analysis.one_liner: Lets health insurers sell individual policies nationwide under the rules of whichever state they choose.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2009 with two Republican sponsors and never advanced: it was referred to the Senate committee that handles health policy and received no hearing, vote, or further action before that Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change who regulates health insurance sold to individuals. Today, each state sets its own rules for plans sold to its residents — what benefits must be covered, how premiums can be set, and what protections buyers get. Under this bill, an insurer could pick one state as its 'primary state' and sell its individual policies in every other state under those primary-state rules, escaping the local state's requirements, except for a short list of financial and claims-handling rules that still apply. Supporters pitched it as a way to lower premiums by letting insurers avoid costly state mandates; the same mechanism would let insurers sell plans that skip the benefits and consumer protections a buyer's own state requires.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual-market insurance buyers who are healthy and want a lower-premium, bare-bones plan would gain the most, since insurers could base plans in states with fewer mandated benefits and lighter rating rules. Insurers would gain a major new choice: instead of complying with 50 different sets of state rules, they could pick the friendliest one and sell everywhere.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Healthy buyers seeking cheaper plans; insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill's stated findings say the many differences in state law impede insurers from offering and individuals from obtaining affordable individual health insurance, and it cites multi-state insurance models as a precedent [S3].

An insurer would designate one 'primary state' whose covered laws govern its individual policies in that state and every other state, and it would be exempt from any secondary state's laws that prohibit or regulate its operation [S2][S3].

The bill's required disclosure notice tells buyers the policy may be less expensive precisely because it is not subject to all of the buyer's state's insurance laws, including coverage of some state-mandated services and the state's consumer protection and rate-change restrictions [S3].

It is not a total deregulation: insurers selling across state lines must be licensed in a primary state that uses a risk-based capital formula for solvency [S3], must give buyers an independent external appeal of denied claims [S3], remain subject to secondary-state rules on taxes, financial examinations, guaranty-fund participation, fraud, and unfair claims settlement practices [S3], and cannot reclassify an individual or raise their premium at renewal based on health status [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Buyers who need the benefits their own state mandates — including many people with pre-existing conditions — would bear the cost if the plans offered under this bill exclude those services, since medical underwriting and rating would be governed by whichever state the insurer picks. State insurance regulators would lose most of their authority over plans sold to their residents, retaining only a narrow list of enforcement tools.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions; state regulators

drawbacks.text: Insurers could base themselves in the state with the weakest rules and sell those policies everywhere, so a resident of a state that requires, say, maternity or mental health coverage could be sold a plan that does not cover them — a tradeoff the bill's own mandated disclosure language acknowledges [S3].

The bill keeps HIPAA guaranteed-availability rules for eligible individuals only in narrow situations [S3], and 'covered laws' governing rating expressly include medical underwriting by the primary state [S3], meaning plans sold under this bill need not cover pre-existing conditions unless the primary state's rules require it; the bill orders a government study of exactly how people with pre-existing conditions would fare [S3].

Because leaner, cheaper plans appeal most to healthy people, sicker people could be left in a smaller, more expensive risk pool — a standard consequence when a low-regulation product competes for the healthy while comprehensive plans keep the sick; the bill's required annual study would track effects on the number of uninsured and underinsured and on premiums generally [S3].
Sole enforcement jurisdiction over the primary state's rules would sit with the primary state [S2][S3], so a buyer in a secondary state would depend on a distant regulator to police their policy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine upside is real but narrow: healthy individual-market buyers could see cheaper premiums, and the bill does build in some federal guardrails (solvency standards, external appeals, limits on health-status re-rating at renewal). But the design rewards insurers for choosing the most permissive regulator, strips most state oversight of policies sold to local residents, offers no general protection for pre-existing conditions, and its own text concedes the plans would lack buyer-state benefits and consumer protections. An honest weighing finds the savings concentrated among the healthy while the risks fall on the sick and on state-level consumer protections.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's health committee in July 2009, and that is where it stayed — no hearing, no vote, and no further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim DeMint (R-SC), joined by Sen. David Vitter (R-LA), introduced the bill on July 16, 2009, during the national debate over the Affordable Care Act [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The committee took no further action of any kind, and the bill carried only one cosponsor [S4][S5].
The bill died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2011, never having received a vote in committee or on the Senate floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, nothing changed: state insurance regulators kept their full authority over individual-market plans sold to their residents, and the insurers' existing state-by-state regulatory obligations were untouched. The bill arrived during the ACA debate with almost no cosponsors, so its death reflects a lack of support rather than a defeat of a popular measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State regulators; existing consumer protections stayed intact

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor

against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — so the bill sat until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: Both of its sponsors were Republicans and it drew a single cosponsor; it died in a committee controlled by Democrats, so support ran entirely on one side of the aisle.

industries.note: The bill would let insurers pick their own regulator and sell nationwide in the individual market, escaping state benefit mandates and rate restrictions — a regulatory advantage that supports leaner, cheaper plans. The same freedom cuts both ways for the industry's customers: cheaper skinnier plans for the healthy, weaker guarantees for the sick.

Secondary states would lose most authority over individual policies sold to their residents, keeping only a short list of powers (taxes, solvency exams, guaranty funds, fraud and claims-practice enforcement). Their interest here runs with consumers', since they are the ones currently enforcing state benefit mandates and rating rules.
